summary:
Exploring Mars is not just about reaching a destination. Astronauts must navigate challenging terrain while managing limited oxygen, battery power, and time.

Marsel Navigator is an interactive mission-planning prototype that helps astronauts choose routes based on their mission priorities while considering terrain-related risks and resource constraints.

Using real elevation data from Jezero Crater, our system calculates alternative round-trip routes with a terrain-aware A* algorithm. Astronauts can select a scientific objective, enter their available resources, and prioritize saving time, avoiding steep slopes, or balancing resources. Marsel Navigator compares the alternatives and provides an explainable recommendation.

Our platform also offers multiple 2D terrain views and connects to an interactive Unity environment, allowing users to visualize selected routes and explore the Martian landscape in 3D.

By transforming complex planetary data into accessible mission-planning decisions, Marsel Navigator addresses the challenge of making Mars exploration more informed and practical. As a research prototype, it has potential applications in astronaut training, mission simulations, and planetary science education.

Our vision is simple: help future explorers go further while planning a safer journey home.
details:
Imagine an astronaut exploring Mars. A scientific destination might be only a few kilometers away, but reaching it involves much more than finding the shortest path.

Steep slopes, challenging terrain, limited oxygen, battery capacity, and mission time all influence the journey. A shorter route may expose astronauts to more demanding terrain, while a gentler route may require more time and resources.

The challenge is to identify a route that supports the astronaut's mission priorities while accounting for terrain-related risks and the resources required to return.

Our Solution

Marsel Navigator is an interactive, terrain-aware mission-planning prototype developed for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge.

Our goal is to make complex mission planning understandable and accessible.

Astronauts can select a scientific objective, enter available resources, and choose a mission priority: Save Time, Avoid Steep Slopes, or Balance Resources.

The application evaluates alternative routes and recommends a feasible option based on the selected priorities and modeled resource constraints. Rather than presenting a route without explanation, Marsel Navigator shows the reasoning behind its recommendation, allowing users to understand the trade-offs.

How It Works

Marsel Navigator uses real elevation data from Jezero Crater, the landing site of NASA's Perseverance rover.

We use a measured terrain model derived from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Context Camera (CTX) observations, with approximately 20-meter grid spacing in our study area.

A terrain-aware A pathfinding algorithm* calculates route alternatives based on distance and slope exposure.

The system evaluates the complete mission, including travel from a hypothetical habitat to a scientific destination and the return journey.

For each calculated alternative, Marsel Navigator estimates:

  • Round-trip distance and travel time
  • Oxygen consumption using illustrative research units
  • Battery usage
  • Exposure to steep terrain
  • Feasibility under available resources and required reserves

Users can explore the Martian landscape through multiple 2D map layers, including orbital imagery, elevation, and derived slope.

From 2D Planning to Interactive 3D Exploration

One of our most distinctive features is the connection between our Python-based route planner and a Unity 3D environment.

A selected route can be transferred through a working local connection and visualized on the Martian terrain. Users can control an astronaut, explore the landscape, and experience the route from a ground-level perspective.

This creates a connection between scientific terrain data, route calculations, and interactive exploration.

Our web interface is also touch-friendly, making the planning experience accessible on mobile devices.

Technology and Development

We developed Marsel Navigator using:

  • Python for terrain analysis, route calculations, and resource modeling
  • Streamlit for the interactive web application
  • A pathfinding* for terrain-aware route generation
  • USGS CTX elevation data and NASA mission resources for the Jezero study area
  • Unity and C# for the interactive 3D environment and astronaut controls
  • Local HTTP/JSON communication for transferring calculated routes from Python to Unity
  • GitLab for version control and collaboration

Creativity and Intended Impact

Marsel Navigator goes beyond displaying planetary maps by transforming scientific data into an explainable planning decision.

Its central innovation is combining mission priorities, real terrain analysis, round-trip resource estimates, and interactive 3D visualization within a single workflow.

We designed the system around an important principle: astronauts should be able to understand why a particular route is recommended rather than simply follow an algorithm.

The prototype has potential applications in astronaut training simulations, mission-planning research, and planetary science education. It can help users better understand how human needs and environmental constraints interact during planetary exploration.

Limitations and Future Vision

Marsel Navigator is a research prototype, not an operational or flight-certified astronaut safety system.

Our oxygen and battery models use illustrative assumptions rather than calibrated life-support specifications. The terrain dataset also cannot identify every small rock, local obstacle, or environmental hazard.

Future development would include more detailed hazard information, improved resource models, and additional validation.

Our long-term vision is to develop Marsel Navigator into a real-time navigation companion — like Google Maps for Mars — where the map follows the astronaut's movement and helps them stay on course as mission conditions change.

Our Mission

We believe successful Mars exploration is not only about how far humanity can travel, but also about making informed decisions throughout the journey.

Marsel Navigator — Explore Further. Return Safer.
